report.source_text: Six weeks after stem cell transplant for myelodysplastic syndrome, a 51 year old caucasian patient developed a high-grade pure motor flaccid tetraparesis within a few days. While cognitive and brainstem functions – including the function of facial muscles – were preserved, the patient was tetraplegic except for minimal finger movements of the left hand. The deep tendon reflexes were absent, and Babinski testing revealed mute soles on both sides. There was considerable generalized muscle atrophy which had already been noticed at first neurological assessment five days before transplant.

report.source_text: A few days later, however, an acute confusional state prompted brain MRI. Fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) imaging revealed symmetrical hyperintensities strictly limited to the subcortical precentral gyrus (Fig. 1a). Correspondingly, diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) showed signal hyperintensity (Fig. 1b), along with normal ADC and without any contrast enhancement. Six days before transplant, the patient had received cranial MRI without any pathological finding. Thus, tetraplegia was attributable to new symmetrical CNS lesions.

report.source_text: Accordingly, intravenous ganciclovir treatment (5 mg per kg per day over two weeks) was initiated. Over the following three weeks, serum PCR for CMV turned negative. Tetraparesis slowly improved, with still moderate pareses of the upper (between MRC 3 and 4), but severe pareses of the lower (between MRC 1 and 2) extremities at neurological reassessment four weeks after symptom onset. Unfortunately, in the further course the patient developed a septic syndrome, most likely owing to a pulmonary focus, and exspired due to septic multiple organ failure.

clinician.final_diagnosis: CMV encephalitis with tetraplegia in an immunocompromised post-stem cell transplant patient
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 51-year-old patient with myelodysplastic syndrome underwent stem cell transplant and was placed on strong immunosuppression (cyclosporine A and mycophenolate mofetil). Six weeks post-transplant, the patient developed acute-onset high-grade pure motor flaccid tetraparesis within a few days, with preserved cognitive and brainstem functions. Neurological examination revealed tetraplegic status with minimal finger movements of the left hand, absent deep tendon reflexes bilaterally, and mute Babinski responses. An acute confusional state prompted brain MRI, which revealed new symmetrical hyperintensities strictly limited to the subcortical precentral gyrus on FLAIR imaging with corresponding DWI signal hyperintensity, normal ADC, and no contrast enhancement. Prior MRI 6 days before transplant had been normal. CSF analysis showed normal cell count (1 leucocyte/mm³) with slightly elevated protein (56.2 mg/dl) and albumin (50.9 mg/dl), but CSF PCR was negative for CMV and other neurotropic viruses. However, serum CMV PCR showed progressive increase up to 8,600 copies/ml starting shortly before tetraparesis development. Intravenous ganciclovir (5 mg/kg/day for two weeks) was initiated. Over the following three weeks, serum CMV PCR turned negative and tetraparesis slowly improved, with moderate pareses of upper extremities (MRC 3-4) and severe pareses of lower extremities (MRC 1-2) at four-week reassessment. The patient subsequently developed septic syndrome from a pulmonary focus and expired from septic multiple organ failure.
